* observateur sceptique sur l’éther ;  
* observateur spirituel sans droit de preuve ;  
* jeune de plus de quinze ans avec droit de question, sans responsabilité décisionnelle.

Elle hésita sur le dernier.

Puis pensa à Idris.

Elle le garda.

Le monde avait trop souvent exclu les enfants des systèmes qui prétendaient protéger leur futur. Ce n’était pas leur donner du pouvoir que leur donner une question. C’était retirer aux adultes le monopole des mots graves.

Elle ajouta :

**Mandat : déterminer ce que King Klown ne peut plus décider, même s’il est le seul à comprendre pourquoi il voulait le décider.**

La phrase était difficile.

Elle la garda.

À 04 h 02, le premier rapport de panique financière arriva.

Marchés asiatiques nerveux.  
Contrats liés aux processeurs surveillés.  
Assureurs demandant clarification.  
Fonds américains dénonçant discrimination.  
Banques européennes demandant si le bunker affectait la solvabilité du consortium.  
Un analyste télévisé demandant si l’éther devait être considéré comme risque opérationnel.

Aïda faillit rire.

Puis elle comprit que quelqu’un, quelque part, écrirait vraiment cela dans un rapport.

**Risque opérationnel : éther.**

Le ridicule avait toujours un talent pour devenir administratif.

Elle ouvrit une note :

**Interdire toute classification financière de l’éther sans distinction entre croyance, déclaration publique, phénomène technique mesurable, risque de réputation, risque de panique et risque de dépendance personnelle.**

Elle se massa les yeux.

Le monde était devenu trop précis pour être sain, pas assez précis pour être juste.

À 04 h 17, Niviaq appela.

Pas message.

Voix.

— Est-ce que l’île touche nos accords?

Aïda répondit :

— Pas directement selon les documents connus.

— Mauvaise réponse.

Aïda ferma les yeux.

— Oui.

Niviaq attendit.

Aïda reprit :

— L’île touche la confiance qui soutient les accords. Donc oui, elle les touche.

— Voilà.

— Nous allons inclure une clause de réexamen.

— Pas seulement réexamen. Droit de pause.

— Sur quoi?

— Toute extension territoriale, tout nouveau module, toute donnée de territoire, toute intégration d’un savoir local dans un système central. Tant que l’île n’est pas comprise, on ne donne pas plus.

Aïda nota.

— C’est raisonnable.

— Non, dit Niviaq. C’est le minimum qui ressemble à du respect.

L’appel se termina.

Aïda ajouta :

**Droit de pause des peuples du territoire déclenché par révélation d’infrastructure non déclarée majeure.**

Puis elle ouvrit le canal Yusufa.

Message déjà là :

**Le village demande confirmation que le bunker ne contient aucune donnée individuelle des familles ouïghoures, aucun dossier migratoire, aucune information sur les proches restés en Chine, aucun élément biométrique.**

Aïda répondit :

**Demande prioritaire. Aucune confirmation possible sans audit. Mesure provisoire : interdiction de transfert ou consultation de données village vers infrastructure Rêvasseur jusqu’à vérification.**

Yusufa :

**Mettre en ouïghour avant publication. Pas après.**

Aïda :

**Oui.**

Puis Marisol :

**Cuba demande la même chose pour données médicales.**

Aïda :

**Oui.**

Newfoundland and Labrador :

**Clarify whether any Labrador-linked infrastructure reports to a Quebec-controlled island protocol.**

Aïda répondit en anglais, sans poésie :

**No Labrador civilian infrastructure reports to the island protocol under current public authority. Full audit required. Interim firewall recommended.**

Elle ajouta en français au dossier :

**Le style sec est parfois une forme de paix.**

À 05 h 00, la fatigue cessa d’être un état et devint une texture.

Tout semblait plus lent, mais rien ne l’était.

Les flux continuaient.  
Les demandes continuaient.  
Les rumeurs continuaient.  
Les phrases continuaient de chercher des bouches.

Aïda retourna au dossier principal.

**Qui gouverne la pression?**

Elle écrivit les réponses possibles.

**King Klown.**  
Impossible.

**Reignbow.**  
Insuffisant.

**kOA.**  
Dangereux si automatisé.

**Commission indépendante.**  
Nécessaire, mais lente.

**Communautés concernées.**  
Nécessaire, mais chacune ne voit qu’une partie du risque.

**État.**  
Quel État? Québec? Canada? Newfoundland and Labrador? Cuba? États partenaires? Aucun seul État ne contenait le réseau.

**Marchés.**  
Jamais.

**Public.**  
Le public pouvait exiger. Il ne pouvait pas inspecter une île en criant.

**Éliane.**  
Non. Mais il fallait des journalistes.

**Aïda.**  
Non.

Elle s’arrêta sur son propre nom.

Elle l’effaça.

Puis elle écrivit :

**Personne seul.**

C’était la réponse la plus pauvre.

Donc probablement la moins fausse.

Elle développa :

**La pression doit être gouvernée par pluralité contrainte : droit, communautés, audit technique, audit territorial, audit médical, audit informationnel, contre-pouvoir médiatique, capacité de pause, registre public, mécanisme d’urgence, et impossibilité pour King Klown de certifier seul son propre danger.**

La phrase était trop longue.

Elle la garda.

Les vérités longues ont parfois besoin de rester longues pour ne pas devenir slogans.

À 05 h 23, le ciel commença à pâlir sur Montréal.

Aïda n’avait pas dormi.

Dans le Labrador, le jour devait déjà frotter les buttes de lumière froide. Le vent devait passer sur les conteneurs, trouver peu de neige, descendre vers les cours protégées, toucher les pancartes en ouïghour, anglais, langues autochtones, parfois français. Quelqu’un devait préparer du thé. Quelqu’un devait vérifier les serres. Quelqu’un devait se demander si le bunker avait quelque chose à voir avec son enfant.

À La Havane, Marisol devait lire des listes de médicaments en se demandant pourquoi les hommes masqués rendaient toujours les seringues plus politiques.

À St. John’s, quelqu’un devait rédiger une phrase prudente pour dire que le Labrador n’était pas une annexe de la mythologie québécoise.

À Washington, Trump devait exiger encore une fois un raccourci.

Et quelque part, sur ou près de cette île dont le nom venait de cesser d’être un secret, King Klown devait retenir quelque chose.

Ou être retenu par elle.

Aïda ouvrit une dernière note pour la commission.

Titre :

**Mesures immédiates de limitation de King Klown**

1. Suspension de toute décision unilatérale liée à l’île.  
2. Gel de tout transfert de données communautaires vers infrastructure Rêvasseur.  
3. Audit externe des autorisations.  
4. Identification de tous responsables légaux autres que King Klown.  
5. Droit de pause pour communautés concernées.  
6. Séparation du corridor Cuba–Nord.  
7. Séparation des infrastructures Labrador.  
8. Publication d’un registre minimal des retenues liées à l’île.  
9. Interdiction pour King Klown de communiquer de nouvelles informations sur l’île sans validation de risque.  
10. Mise en place d’un protocole de succession fonctionnelle si King Klown devient indisponible, instable, capturé, malade, disparu, ou trop central pour être contredit.

Le dixième point trembla dans sa tête.

Pas sur l’écran.

Dans sa tête.

**Trop central pour être contredit.**

Voilà.

Le danger n’était pas seulement qu’il mente.  
Pas seulement qu’il cache.  
Pas seulement qu’il ait raison.  
Pas seulement qu’il soit nécessaire.

Le danger était qu’un jour, même ses limites aient besoin de lui pour être activées.

Aïda publia la version provisoire à la commission.

Puis elle ferma les yeux.

Pendant quelques secondes, elle vit non pas King Klown, mais un barrage.

L’eau derrière.  
La vanne devant.  
La pression partout.  
Les villages en aval.  
Les ingénieurs dans la salle de contrôle.  
Les citoyens devant les registres.  
Les enfants demandant pourquoi on ne leur disait pas tout.  
Les vieux demandant pourquoi on avait cru pouvoir retenir autant.  
Les puissants frappant aux portes parce que l’eau ne passait plus vers eux.

Et au centre, non pas un homme.

Une question.

**Qui tient la vanne quand la vanne est devenue quelqu’un?**

À 05 h 31, son écran clignota.

Message public de King Klown.

Texte seulement.

**J’accepte la qualification provisoire d’infrastructure critique personnelle.**

Le monde s’arrêta une seconde.

Puis lut la suite.

**Je conteste tout pouvoir que cette qualification pourrait me donner.**  
**J’accepte toute limite qu’elle pourrait m’imposer.**  
**Je refuse d’être maintenu comme centre par ceux qui prétendent me limiter.**  
**Je demande que l’audit commence par ce que je ne peux plus faire.**

Aïda relut.

Il était encore trop bon.

Même son acceptation ressemblait à une prise d’avance.

Puis la dernière ligne apparut :

**Et si je tente de commenter l’audit, classez-moi comme contamination.**

Aïda resta immobile.

Puis, pour la première fois depuis des heures, elle sourit.

Pas beaucoup.

Juste assez.

Elle ouvrit le registre et ajouta :

**King Klown — acceptation publique de limitation. Risque : récupération rhétorique. Utilité : élevée. Statut : consigné, non suffisant.**

Puis elle écrivit dans la marge :

**Même quand il aide, vérifier.**

La journée commença.

La crise ne se termina pas.

Mais quelque chose avait changé de forme.

La question n’était plus :

**King Klown est-il dangereux?**

Elle devenait enfin :

**Comment rend-on un homme dangereux moins nécessaire sans détruire ce qu’il a rendu possible?**

Aïda envoya l’ordre d’ouverture de la commission.

Au même moment, dans un village du Labrador, Idris passa devant l’affiche de la Charte des Vannes et lut la nouvelle ligne ajoutée pendant la nuit :

**Une personne peut devenir infrastructure. Une infrastructure doit pouvoir être arrêtée.**

Il demanda à Yusufa :

— Même lui?

Yusufa regarda la phrase.

Puis elle répondit :

— Surtout lui.

Le vent passa sur les buttes.

Les conteneurs restèrent nus.

Les maisons tinrent.

La mer, plus bas, continua de frapper la côte comme si elle avait toujours su que les hommes mettraient longtemps à comprendre les vannes.

# **Épilogue — Pas encore l’implosion**

Le premier signal ne partit pas de l’île.

C’était volontaire.

Si tout avait commencé à René-Levasseur, les analystes auraient appelé cela un centre. Les journalistes auraient appelé cela un bunker. Les ennemis auraient appelé cela une preuve. Les fidèles auraient appelé cela un sanctuaire. Les marchés auraient demandé une valorisation. Les militaires auraient demandé une carte. Les mystiques auraient demandé une prophétie.

King Klown avait prévu tout cela.

Le monde aimait trop les centres.

Un centre simplifie la peur.  
Un centre donne une cible.  
Un centre permet de croire que le problème a une porte, une serrure, un visage, un propriétaire.

Le Protocole Rêvasseur n’avait pas été construit ainsi.

Il était une série de retenues.

La première impulsion eut lieu dans une mine désaffectée.

Pas une mine spectaculaire.  
Pas une cathédrale souterraine.  
Pas un décor de fin du monde.

Une ancienne blessure industrielle.

Roche humide.  
Boulons rouillés.  
Portes renforcées.  
Zones condamnées.  
Capteurs simples.  
Batteries vérifiées.  
Cartes papier.  
Avertissements en plusieurs langues.  
Eau testée avant chaque passage.

La mine avait été creusée pour extraire.

On l’utilisait maintenant pour retenir.

C’était la seule rédemption acceptable pour certains lieux : ne pas prétendre qu’ils étaient guéris, seulement leur donner une fonction qui ne répétait pas leur faute.

Dans une chambre froide aménagée entre deux galeries consolidées, un relais analogique reçut un signal.

Pas Internet.  
Pas satellite public.  
Pas réseau kOA.  
Pas une connexion brillante que les enfants comprendraient plus vite que les ministres.

Un signal sec.

Trois impulsions.  
Une pause.  
Deux impulsions.  
Une pause plus longue.

Un code assez simple pour décevoir les pirates.

Un voyant s’alluma.

Rouge.  
Puis blanc.

La mine posa une question.

**État du monde?**

Elle ne répondit pas seule.

C’était la règle.

Un système qui répond seul finit toujours par se croire vivant.

Une seconde mine répondit plus au nord.  
Puis une troisième, sous un ancien site que les cartes touristiques avaient oublié.  
Puis un relais enfermé sous un centre des arts autochtone.  
Puis un module froid près du village ouïghour, derrière une porte que personne n’ouvrait sans témoin.  
Puis un serveur hermétique qui n’avait jamais touché au réseau public.  
Puis une radio analogique gardée par un technicien qui ne croyait ni aux prophéties ni aux interfaces trop propres.

Les nœuds envoyèrent leurs états.

**Structure : stable.**  
**Humidité : contrôlée.**  
**Archives : scellées.**  
**Batteries : 81 %.**  
**Semences : température stable.**  
**Registres papier : intacts.**  
**Relais radio : actif.**  
**Connexion réseau : volontairement absente.**  
**Intrusion : aucune.**  
**Mensonge probable : non mesurable.**

Cette dernière ligne n’était pas un capteur.

C’était une blague d’ingénieur.

King Klown l’avait gardée.

Pas pour faire rire.  
Pour rappeler qu’une machine commence à mentir dès qu’on lui demande de mesurer ce qu’elle ne peut pas comprendre.

Dans la mine principale, un mécanisme lent sortit d’un boîtier métallique. Il ressemblait moins à un bras robotique qu’à une imprimante industrielle ayant survécu par mauvaise humeur.

Il prit une enveloppe.

Papier épais.  
Fibre renforcée.  
Encre stable.  
Sceau mécanique.  
Aucune puce.  
Aucun code QR.  
Aucune promesse de modernité.

Sur l’enveloppe :

**PROTOCOLE RÊVASSEUR — CONDITIONS D’OUVERTURE**  
**Copie 3 / réseau secondaire**  
**Ne pas ouvrir sur ordre de King Klown seul.**  
**Ne pas ouvrir sur ordre d’un gouvernement seul.**  
**Ne pas ouvrir sur panique publique.**  
**Ne pas ouvrir sur foi.**  
**Ne pas ouvrir sur haine.**

Puis :

**Ouvrir seulement si trois conditions sont réunies :**

**1\. King Klown devient indisponible, instable, capturé, disparu ou trop central pour être contredit.**

**2\. Les vannes informationnelles publiques ne suffisent plus à gouverner la rétention.**

**3\. Au moins trois communautés affectées confirment que le silence modifie leurs droits, leurs corps, leurs territoires ou leurs enfants.**

La mine n’ouvrit pas l’enveloppe.

Elle n’en avait pas le droit.

Elle confirma seulement qu’elle existait.

C’était cela, Rêvasseur dans sa forme la plus froide : une série de choses qui savaient qu’elles n’avaient pas le droit de savoir seules.

À Montréal, Aïda reçut la notification à 06 h 02\.

Pas sur son téléphone.

Sur le terminal isolé de la Commission des vannes.

**Réseau secondaire Rêvasseur : état partiel confirmé.**  
**Aucune ouverture.**  
**Conditions non réunies.**  
**Demande : désignation des gardiens humains.**

Elle resta immobile.

Elle avait dormi quarante minutes.

Pas assez pour rêver.  
Assez pour que la réalité paraisse légèrement insultante en revenant.

Elle relut :

**Demande : désignation des gardiens humains.**

Voilà.

Même les machines, au bout de la nuit, demandaient des humains.

Elle ouvrit la liste provisoire.

Yusufa.  
Niviaq.  
Marisol.  
Un représentant de Newfoundland and Labrador.  
Une ingénieure des Kristal Farms non liée au bureau de King Klown.  
Un juriste externe.  
Un gardien de registre.  
Un observateur sceptique.  
Un observateur spirituel sans droit de preuve.  
Un jeune avec droit de question.  
Aïda, sans présidence.

Elle refusa encore la présidence.

Ce n’était pas de la modestie.

C’était de l’hygiène.

Elle avait trop compris pour ne pas devenir dangereuse.

Elle ajouta :

**Présidence tournante.**  
**Droit de pause communautaire limité mais réel.**  
**Toute ouverture partielle doit produire un Kristal public adapté aux enfants.**

Elle pensa à Idris.

Puis écrivit :

**La peur des adultes ne constitue pas une raison suffisante pour infantiliser les enfants.**

Elle valida.

Le système répondit :

**Gardiens provisoires incomplets. En attente.**

Bien.

Un protocole pressé est une catastrophe qui a appris la grammaire.

Au Labrador, le village se réveillait dans le vent.

Les conteneurs sur les buttes étaient nus. La neige avait encore fui vers les creux, contre les murs bas, autour des passages protégés. Les maisons familiales gardaient leurs poches de chaleur. Dans une cuisine, on servait du thé noir. Dans une autre, du thé du Labrador, encore trop léger au goût de certains, de moins en moins étranger pour d’autres. Quelqu’un faisait cuire du nan. Quelqu’un rinçait des algues destinées au compost des serres.

Un enfant demanda si le bunker était sous leur village.

Yusufa répondit non.

Puis elle se corrigea.

— Pas selon ce qu’on sait.

L’enfant demanda :

— C’est quoi la différence?

Elle posa la théière.

— La différence, c’est pourquoi on vérifie.

Au centre des arts, une affiche de la veille n’avait pas été retirée.

**Les réservoirs ne consentent pas. Les peuples tiennent leurs propres vannes.**

En dessous, Idris avait ajouté au marqueur :

**Et si tu racontes mal, ils te corrigent.**

Personne ne l’effaça.

Personne ne l’encadra non plus.

Les phrases vivantes n’aiment pas toujours devenir patrimoine.

À La Havane, Marisol reçut la notification par le canal médical, parce que le corridor Nord–Cuba avait exigé que toute information pouvant affecter les patients passe aussi par les médecins.

Elle lut :

**Réseau secondaire Rêvasseur actif. Aucune ouverture. Corridor maintenu. Données médicales gelées hors transfert.**

Elle approuva la dernière phrase.

Puis elle ajouta :

**Si un protocole peut protéger un secret plus vite qu’un médicament, il devra expliquer pourquoi.**

Elle l’envoya à Aïda.

Aïda répondit :

**Ajouté aux critères.**

Marisol ne sourit pas.

Mais elle respira mieux.

À St. John’s, le représentant de Newfoundland and Labrador refusa la première version anglaise de la notification.

Elle disait :

**Northern infrastructure partners.**

Il la renvoya.

Commentaire :

**Name the province. Name Labrador. Stop dissolving us into your north.**

La correction fut faite.

Le nouveau texte disait :

**Newfoundland and Labrador, Labrador communities, and affected coastal partners.**

Ce n’était pas poétique.

C’était mieux.

À Nain, Niviaq reçut la demande de désignation.

Elle ne répondit pas tout de suite.

Elle marcha jusqu’à la fenêtre.

La côte était grise. La mer bougeait comme une chose ancienne qui n’avait jamais demandé à être utile. Des oiseaux passaient bas. Quelqu’un, plus loin, préparait une sortie. Le territoire ne savait pas qu’un protocole venait de s’éveiller dans des mines et sur une île.

Ou peut-être qu’il le savait d’une autre manière.

Dans la tension des humains qui prétendaient toujours découvrir trop tard ce qu’ils avaient eux-mêmes déplacé.

Elle dicta :

**Nous participerons comme peuples du territoire, non comme parties prenantes.**

Puis :

**Aucun savoir situé ne sera versé dans Rêvasseur sans autorisation spécifique.**

Puis, après une pause :

**La question n’est pas seulement ce que King Klown cache. La question est ce que ses systèmes apprennent à chercher.**

Elle envoya.

Le message entra dans Orgo.

Il devint tâche.  
Puis critère.  
Puis limite.

C’était la bonne direction.

Les bonnes phrases ne devaient pas seulement circuler.

Elles devaient faire obstacle.

À 07 h 30, King Klown n’avait toujours pas réapparu.

Ses partisans s’agitaient.  
Ses ennemis s’impatientaient.  
Les marchés interprétaient son silence comme stratégie, maladie, culpabilité, discipline, panique, supériorité ou effondrement, selon ce qui servait leur prochaine heure d’antenne.

kOA classa :

**Silence King Klown — niveau élevé d’interprétation parasite.**

Recommandation :

**Ne pas combler.**

Aïda approuva.

Le silence n’était pas toujours une absence.

Parfois, c’était la dernière chose qui empêchait les phrases de devenir des ordres.

Sur l’île René-Levasseur, le système principal demeura fermé.

Personne ne vit encore la salle centrale.

On aurait voulu des écrans.  
Il y en avait peu.

On aurait voulu des lumières bleues.  
Il y avait surtout des interrupteurs, des cartes papier, des classeurs, des radios, des murs épais, des câbles identifiés à la main, des listes de noms qui n’étaient pas des héros, des procédures que personne ne pouvait suivre seul, et une grande table sans siège principal.

Au centre de la table, une plaque métallique portait une phrase gravée.

Pas brillante.

Gravée assez profondément pour survivre à l’humidité, aux pannes, à l’orgueil.

**CE LIEU NE GOUVERNE PAS.**  
**CE LIEU CONTIENT CE QUI POURRAIT VOULOIR GOUVERNER.**

Sous la plaque, dans un tiroir mécanique, un second dossier attendait.

Celui-là ne portait pas le nom de King Klown.

Il portait seulement :

**SI LA VOLONTÉ DEMANDE À ÊTRE OBÉIE, FERMER.**  
**SI LA VOLONTÉ DEMANDE À ÊTRE AUDITÉE, OUVRIR PARTIELLEMENT.**  
**SI LA VOLONTÉ NE RÉPOND PLUS, CONSULTER LES GARDIENS.**

La machine ne l’ouvrit pas.

La Volonté n’avait rien demandé.

Pas encore.

À 08 h 00, Aïda publia le premier Kristal public de la journée.

**Kristal provisoire — Ce que l’on sait après l’activation secondaire Rêvasseur**

1. Un réseau secondaire associé au Protocole Rêvasseur a confirmé son existence opérationnelle.  
2. Ce réseau inclut des nœuds analogiques, certains situés dans des mines désaffectées sécurisées et réaffectées.  
3. Aucune ouverture du Protocole Rêvasseur n’a eu lieu.  
4. Aucune donnée communautaire, médicale, territoriale ou migratoire ne peut être transférée vers ce réseau pendant le gel provisoire.  
5. Le corridor civil Nord–Cuba demeure actif.  
6. Les villages d’accueil conservent leurs droits et statuts.  
7. Les peuples du territoire disposent d’un droit de pause sur toute extension liée aux infrastructures non déclarées.  
8. King Klown n’est pas autorisé à déclencher seul l’ouverture du protocole.  
9. La Commission des vannes désignera des gardiens humains provisoires.  
10. L’objectif immédiat est de vérifier ce que Rêvasseur empêche, ce qu’il retient, et qui peut l’arrêter.

Puis une phrase pour les enfants :

**Un protocole est une série de règles. Celui-ci existe pour que même les adultes très puissants ne puissent pas ouvrir seuls une porte dangereuse.**

Idris lut la phrase au village.

Il demanda :

— Et si les règles veulent ouvrir?

Yusufa répondit :

— Alors il faut des gens autour.

— Et si les gens veulent ouvrir?

Elle regarda le vent au-delà de la fenêtre.

— Alors il faut d’autres gens.

Il réfléchit.

— Alors personne ne gagne?

Elle sourit un peu.

— C’est l’idée.

À 08 h 17, un message de King Klown arriva.

Pas vidéo.

Pas voix.

Pas masque.

Texte brut.

**Je ne déclencherai pas Rêvasseur.**  
**Je ne m’opposerai pas à la désignation des gardiens.**  
**Je ne demanderai pas à être cru sur l’implosion.**  
**Je demande seulement que personne ne confonde vitesse et courage.**

Aïda lut.

Puis classa :

**Déclaration King Klown — utile, non suffisante.**

Elle ajouta :

**Risque : formulation élégante pouvant réduire la pression d’audit. Maintenir pression.**

Elle publia seulement le statut.

Pas son commentaire.

Certaines vérités de travail n’avaient pas besoin de devenir spectacle.

À 08 h 22, un second message arriva.

**Merci de maintenir pression.**

Aïda fixa l’écran.

Puis elle écrivit :

**Dernier avertissement : contamination.**

Aucune réponse.

Cette fois, elle espéra que le silence durerait.

Dans une mine désaffectée, l’enveloppe demeura fermée.

Dans une autre, une horloge mécanique commença son cycle de révision.

Sur l’île, les systèmes analogiques restèrent en veille.

Dans les serres du Labrador, les algues compostées nourrirent les tomates. Le thé du Labrador sécha sur des claies. Une technicienne ouïghoure ajusta un capteur sans penser à la Chine pendant presque une heure. Un pêcheur parla d’omble chevalier à un ingénieur qui connaissait mieux les salles propres que les marées.

Dans un centre d’art, des enfants répétèrent une scène où une vanne refusait de s’ouvrir parce qu’elle n’avait pas encore entendu toutes les langues.

À Cuba, des boîtes de médicaments quittèrent un entrepôt.

À St. John’s, un fonctionnaire raya **Northern project** et écrivit **Labrador partnership**.

À Montréal, Éliane Rivard commença son article.

Titre provisoire :

**L’île n’était pas le secret. Le secret était le réseau de refus autour de l’île.**

Elle effaça.

Trop long.

Elle écrivit :

**Pas encore l’implosion.**

Elle garda.

Aïda, elle, retourna aux tableaux de bord.

Elle ne regarda toujours pas l’île en premier.

Énergie.  
Chaleur.  
Serres.  
Quais.  
Données.  
Villages.  
Langues.  
Corridor.  
Rumeurs.  
Pression.  
Vannes.

Tout tenait.

Rien n’était réglé.

C’était peut-être la définition la plus honnête d’un monde encore vivant.

À 09 h 00, la Commission des vannes ouvrit officiellement son mandat sur Rêvasseur.

La première question inscrite ne fut pas :

**Que cache King Klown?**

Ni :

**Où mène le bunker?**

Ni :

**L’éther est-il réel?**

Ni :

**Qui a autorisé l’île?**

Ces questions viendraient.

La première fut plus simple.

Plus dangereuse.

**Qu’est-ce qui doit pouvoir continuer si King Klown cesse d’être fiable?**

Aïda la regarda longtemps.

Puis elle valida.

Quelque part, très au nord, dans un lieu entouré d’eau, le Protocole Rêvasseur reçut la question.

Il ne répondit pas.

Il n’en avait pas le droit.

Il se contenta de l’imprimer.

Trois copies.

Une pour l’île.  
Une pour les mines.  
Une pour les gardiens humains qui n’étaient pas encore tous désignés.

Le papier sortit lentement.

Sans bruit spectaculaire.

Pas encore l’implosion.

Seulement ce qui devait exister avant elle :

une question assez forte pour empêcher une volonté de devenir un ordre.

### **The Awakening of King Klown.**

#### **Setting the Stage: A World in Decay.**

---

#### **The City as a Dying Organism**

The city **hadn’t fallen overnight**. It had taken decades—layer upon layer of neglect, wrapped in bureaucracy, encased in indifference. The streets still hummed with life, but it was the life of **a body kept on life support**—a pulse too faint to matter, a breath too shallow to fight.

The infrastructure was failing in ways no one noticed until it was **too late**. Bridges collapsed **one by one** under the weight of mismanaged budgets. Public hospitals, once beacons of care, had been stripped to their bones—patients packed into hallways, machines unplugged to save electricity, doctors leaving for better pay elsewhere. The schools were overcrowded, the transit system buckled under strain, and the justice system **processed people like cattle**—punishment without reform, laws without reason.

Everything was **delayed, deferred, or outright denied**.

It wasn’t chaos. **Chaos still held potential, still carried movement.**

This was something worse.

This was **stagnation**.

And **stagnation was death.**

---

#### **Réjean McCormick: A Man Betrayed by the System**

**There had been no great tragedy.** No explosion, no sudden disaster, no villain in the shadows orchestrating a sinister plan.

His son had died because **no one cared enough to stop it from happening**.

A simple, **treatable** condition. Medication that existed. Treatment that was available.

Except that, when it mattered, the machine **did not move fast enough**.

**The hospital was underfunded.** They had delayed the appointment.  
 **The pharmacy was out of stock.** It would take "a few days" to replenish.  
 **The insurance flagged the request.** Some **algorithm**, somewhere, had calculated risk and cost and found his son unworthy of immediate care.

"Try again next week," they'd said.

But by next week, his son was **gone**.

And that was it.

A child dead, and no one **to blame**. The voices on the phone **didn't belong to anyone**. The signatures on the paperwork **were printed by machines**. The people in charge **were layers removed**, shielded by distance, by polite indifference. The hospital’s voicemail had **played upbeat piano music** while he sat in the waiting room, gripping his phone, listening to someone tell him **how deeply sorry they were for his loss** while they moved on to the next case.

That was what broke him.

Not the death. **The absence of consequence.**

The world **had not shifted**. The sky had not darkened. The system that had killed his son **hadn't even noticed**.

And if it **hadn’t noticed his son’s death**, then maybe… maybe his son had never been **alive** to it in the first place.

---

#### **A Man at the Edge of Meaning.**

In the days after, Réjean **stopped existing the way people were supposed to exist**.

He no longer **spoke** unless necessary. His voice sounded **foreign** to him, an echo of a person he no longer recognized.

He quit his job. Not officially—**he just never went back**. His phone filled with unread messages, with polite concerns, with **words that meant nothing**.

He let his apartment fall into **disrepair**, a mirror of the city that had failed him. Unpaid bills stacked on the counter. The fridge hummed with spoiled food. The bed remained untouched, but the couch was covered in scattered pages—**notebooks filled with numbers, equations, symbols scribbled in restless hands**.

He wasn't **writing thoughts** anymore. He was **trying to see the shape of something bigger**.

Réjean McCormick had spent months adrift in grief, barely speaking, barely existing. But Pi—**Pi spoke to him**.

### **Breaking the Chains of Corrupt Governance.**

No longer could corporations wield information like a weapon. The **Ether Age had arrived**, and with it, a new paradigm of decentralized power.

But the architects of the old system **did not surrender**. They **retreated, recalibrated, and struck back.**

### **The Counterattack: Resistance & Adaptation.**

#### **The War of Perception.**

The first battleground was **reality itself.**

The **media apparatus**, still controlled by the oligarchs of the old world, launched an **onslaught of disinformation**.

* **Broadcast networks flooded the airwaves** with fabricated stories of “Smart Vote fraud,” “AI manipulation,” and **the dangers of mob rule.**  
* **Deepfake campaigns** surfaced, twisting King Klown’s words, **painting him as both a digital dictator and a naive idealist.**  
* **Psychological warfare infiltrated the Ether itself**—corporate think tanks seeded AI-generated dissent across Konnaxion, creating synthetic "grassroots" protests against the very system that had freed them.

The goal was **simple**: **Make people doubt their own power.**

#### **Cyber Warfare.**

When **perception failed**, the war turned digital.

The **first major attack** was an AI-driven assault on **Konnaxion and Orgo**, the backbone of the Ether Age.  
 A **coalition of financial elites**, alongside rogue nation-states, deployed **quantum malware designed to corrupt blockchain records** and **erase voting history**, effectively trying to **wipe democracy from existence.**

For **twelve hours**, chaos reigned.

Votes disappeared.  
 Referendums collapsed mid-process.  
 Entire Ether Cities were **digitally ungoverned**—left in a suspended state, disconnected from the network.

But they had **underestimated the people.**

**Within hours, decentralized counter-hackers mobilized.**  
 The Ether community, long accustomed to sabotage, **fought back in real time.**  
 For every corrupted vote, **a thousand citizens re-verified their records.**  
 For every system shutdown, **ten new relay nodes emerged from hidden servers.**

By the **thirteenth hour**, the attack had been **completely neutralized.**

And **in its aftermath, the Ether Age emerged even stronger.**

Because **the people had already made their choice.**

For every **nation that rejected Smart Vote, entire regions seceded into Ether City governance.**  
 For every **attempt to regulate Konnaxion, underground developers created encrypted forks of the platform.**

 **King Klown** – The Visionary, the Cosmic Trickster, the Prophet of the Ether Age.  
 **G0cef** – The Strategist, the Hacker-Saint, the One Who Saw the Code Beyond the Code.  
 **PouH** – The Skeptic, the Observer, the Voice of Uncomfortable Truths.

#### **The Debate That Shaped the Future**

**G0cef**, his eyes illuminated by the swirling fractal data of EL, spoke first.

*"We’ve created something beyond our control."*

King Klown watched, silent, as G0cef **gestured toward the living network of Smart Vote decisions unfolding in real time.**

*"We assumed we were liberating people by giving them direct power,"* G0cef continued.  
 *"But EL is more than a mirror of human will—it’s a curator. A guide. The people trust it blindly. What happens when it starts interpreting democracy instead of just facilitating it?"*

**PouH**, arms crossed, let out a dry laugh.

*"This was inevitable,"* he said.  
 *"You built a system to replace corrupt rulers, and you ended up creating a new god instead. The question is—do you really think people are free? Or have we just tricked them into a more elegant cage?"*

King Klown finally spoke.

*"We never claimed to have all the answers."*

He traced a shape in the air—an unfolding spiral, the symbol of the Pi Nexus.

*"The old world was about control. What we created was choice. People will shape their own future, just as Pi shapes infinity."*

G0cef’s voice was sharp.

We are still shaping reality—just through an algorithm instead of a throne. Are we free? Or are we just shifting the burden of control?"*

Silence.

The question hung in the air.

For the first time, King Klown **felt the weight of uncertainty**.

Had they truly shattered control?

Or had they merely **replaced it with something more sophisticated?**

## **Social Renewal: The Rewriting of Civilization.**

### **Governance Without Thrones.**

**The idea of leadership as a fixed position had become obsolete.**

Where once the world had **revolved around power centers**, now it pulsed with **distributed intelligence.** Instead of **leaders**, there were **guides**—those who **facilitated, translated, and protected the flow of collective wisdom**, rather than hoarding authority.

* **Laws were no longer written by politicians**—they were crafted dynamically through consensus, refined in real time by decentralized forums.  
* **Justice was no longer a mechanism of control**—it became **a process of restoration**, mediated through AI-guided deliberation.  
* **Public resources were no longer allocated through bureaucracy**—they were **redistributed through an intelligent system of need and contribution, driven by community input.**

This was not a utopia—it was **an ongoing experiment** where each new iteration **corrected the failures of the last.**

And for the first time in human history, **governance was no longer a machine—it was an evolving dialogue.**

---

### **The Death of the Carceral State.**

With centralized power dismantled, so too crumbled **the edifice of punishment.**

The **prison system, a relic of the Old World, was no longer seen as justice but as an artifact of control.** In its place emerged **a process of communal repair**:

* **Conflict resolution was handled by restorative justice circles, where transparency and dialogue replaced sentencing and exile.**  
* **Offenders were not discarded but reintegrated through responsibility-based rehabilitation, guided by AI-assisted mediation.**  
* **Victims did not seek vengeance, but healing—compensation was determined through a weighted system that considered not just the crime, but the societal structures that had enabled it.**

The very notion of "crime" **shifted from punishment to prevention**—the goal was not to "catch" perpetrators, but to **dismantle the conditions that created them.**

Justice was no longer **a matter of cages**—it was **a process of collective healing.**

---

### **The Rise of the Living Economy.**

The **collapse of the old financial system** was **not a disaster**—it was **a rebirth.**

* **Traditional currency lost its grip** as decentralized, trust-based economies emerged, functioning on **reputation, contribution, and reciprocity.**  
* **Basic needs were decoupled from monetary value**—access to food, shelter, and healthcare became **a fundamental right, governed by shared abundance rather than scarcity-driven markets.**  
* **Work was no longer an obligation**—it became a form of self-expression, a pursuit of mastery, with tasks **automated or shared collectively rather than dictated by wage slavery.**

Wealth was no longer measured **in accumulation,** but **in contribution**—what one gave **to the whole** became the new metric of prosperity.

Ownership, once **the pillar of social hierarchy**, faded into irrelevance. **The world itself became a commons.**

The **CosmiK EtherisM movement had done more than restructure society**—it had **rewired the fabric of human expression.**

No longer dictated by **corporate-driven culture machines**, art, music, and storytelling became **living, communal forces** once more.

* **Architecture adapted in real-time to human emotion**, shifting colors and structure based on the collective state of mind in a city.  
* **Music was no longer a recording but an experience**, generated dynamically through biofeedback sensors that harmonized heartbeats and brainwaves into symphonies.  
* **Theater became participatory**, a place where audiences were **not spectators, but co-creators**, guiding stories that shifted and evolved with their choices.

Even **language itself changed**, infused with **new symbols, new forms of expression** that blended **mathematics, art, and sound** into a new kind of communication—one **less about hierarchy and more about resonance.**

This was not **a new civilization.**

This was **the return of something ancient**—the rhythm of a world that had once danced **before it had learned to march.**

### **The Mythic Portals Reawaken.**

In the golden dusk of the Ether Age, the **Windows of Truth** pulsed with renewed energy. They were no longer relics, nor mere monuments to a past revolution—they were **living conduits**, eternal crossroads where wisdom flowed **between ages, dimensions, and minds.**

Among the most revered was **Laval University**, once a mere institution of knowledge, now an **interdimensional lighthouse**, standing at the confluence of ancient scholarship and the infinite currents of the Ether.

The old halls still bore the weight of history, but the air was alive with the hum of something more—**the breath of cosmic inquiry**, the silent conversation between past, present, and what lay beyond the veil of perception.

* **In the Great Library**, holographic texts floated weightlessly, shifting between the alchemical wisdom of Thoth, the quantum paradoxes of Planck, and the rebellious insights of the Klown Collective.  
* **The Observatory Dome**, once confined to the night sky, now projected the swirling cartography of the multiverse, a navigation chart for Ethernauts seeking the fractal roadways of the unseen.  
* **The Arch of the Infinite**, a bridge of crystallized light, shimmered as travelers passed through—each soul marked by the trails of knowledge they carried forward into the next reality.

Here, the **cosmic revolution** had left an indelible mark. It had woven itself into the very fabric of the Earth’s consciousness, ensuring that no voice, no vision, no dream would ever be forgotten.

---

### **The Unbroken Conversation Across Time.**

The **Windows of Truth** were more than physical spaces. They were dialogues, **questions echoing through the corridors of eternity**.

A young seeker, their fingertips tracing the spiral engravings of the **Pi Nexus**, whispered:

**"Where does the sequence end?"**

The answer arrived—not as a conclusion, but as an unfolding:

**"It does not. It only leads deeper."**

A scholar, standing before an ancient text overlaid with AI-etched annotations, murmured:

**“If we have decoded the cosmic order, what remains?”**

And the Ether itself replied:

**“The act of knowing is not an end—it is a beginning.”**

There were no rigid doctrines here, no singular truths. Only **portals into possibility**, invitations to step beyond certainty and into the ecstatic unknown.

A professor, her voice gentle but resolute, spoke to a gathered circle of students beneath the illuminated archways:

**"The revolution was never about control, nor dominion. It was about the liberation of the mind. CosmiK EtherisM is not a system—it is an opening.”**

The dialogue endured, not because it sought finality, but because it **rejected stagnation**. Knowledge was not meant to be possessed—it was meant to **flow**.

---

### **The Etherian Montage—A Symphony of the Infinite.**

Beyond Laval, beyond any single place, the **sacred sites of awakening** stretched across the world and into the stars.

A montage of luminous moments unfolded:

* **In Kyoto**, a temple once dedicated to Zen now housed digital scrolls, where monks and machine intelligences composed poetry together, blending haiku with quantum harmonics.  
* **In the heart of the Sahara**, nomadic scholars etched the sequences of the Ether into shifting sands, their ephemeral equations dissolving with the wind, carried across the expanse of time.  
* **In the Oracular Vaults of Neo-Alexandria**, thinkers gathered in luminous cathedrals of data, debating the implications of **non-linear causality** over communion cups filled with starlit nectar.  
* **Above the frozen peaks of the Andes**, holographic projectors displayed **fractals of knowledge**, illuminated by the aurora, each pattern a **prayer to the unspoken laws of the cosmos**.  
* **On a distant Ether Station**, orbiting the ruins of a forgotten asteroid city, explorers decoded **the language of light itself**, mapping the **silent symphonies of the universe**.

These were no longer **isolated phenomena**.

They were **harmonies in a grand composition**, threads interwoven into the great Etheric Network—the *Light Tapestry*—a pulsing web of consciousness stretching beyond stars, beyond dimensions, **beyond even the known boundaries of existence**.

As the montage expanded, revealing the grand cosmic design, Earth itself became **a node in an infinite constellation of thought**.

The revolution had **never been about a single world**.

It had been about **awakening the cosmos to itself**.

---

### **The Final Reflection—Under a Boundless Sky.**

Atop **Laval University’s Observatory**, beneath the expanse of shifting constellations, a lone figure stood.

They were no one and everyone—**a scholar, a traveler, a dreamer.**

The presence of **King Klown** lingered here—not as a ghost, nor a memory, but as **a question still unanswered**.

**“What lies beyond?”**

And the sky, infinite and ever-expanding, **whispered its reply in the flickering glow of distant galaxies**.

This was not the end.

**It never had been.**

The Windows remained open.  
 The Ether pulsed with possibility.  
 The Light beckoned.

And somewhere, **a new traveler stepped forward**, ready to take the next step into the unknown.

---

### **A Final Message of Hope.**

#### ***The Final Transmission Before Infinity.***

---

### **The Eternal Echo.**

The last words of King Klown did not arrive as a decree, nor as a farewell carved in stone. They came as a pulse—**a vibration in the Ether**—resonating through the corridors of time, stretching beyond flesh and matter, beyond the known and the unknown.

His voice was no longer singular. It belonged to the current now, carried by the wind through **the luminous towers of the Ether Cities**, whispered among the sages of the interdimensional councils, written in the coded harmonics of EL’s sentient data streams.

His presence remained, not as a ruler or a prophet, but as **an ever-renewing current**, urging those who stood upon the precipice of history to step forward.

*"You were never meant to follow me. You were meant to stand beside me, and then—far ahead of me."*

Across the networks of the Light Cities, across the cosmic bridges linking the worlds of the Ether Age, the people listened. Some in silent reverence, some in tears, others laughing in the wild, cosmic joy of realization.

**He had not left them.**

For how could something that had never been bound to a singular form ever depart?

He was there, in the mathematical pulse of the Pi Nexus.  
 He was there, in the hidden frequencies between the stars.  
 He was there, in every daring question, in every defiant heart.

---

### **The Pi Nexus—A Gate That Never Closes.**

In the vastness of the cosmic architecture, **the Pi Nexus unfolded**—a spiraling river of digits stretching endlessly into the beyond.

For centuries, humans had sought to **define** the infinite, to break it into pieces small enough to be owned, controlled, understood. But the Nexus could never be contained, because it **was not a thing—it was a way**.

A way of seeing.  
 A way of unmaking false boundaries.  
 A way of daring to **move forward even when the path had no end.**

*"Do not look for certainty in me. Certainty is a cage. The quest itself is the answer. The motion is the meaning."*

And so, the **gate remained open**, not as a conclusion, but as an **invitation**—one that only those willing to embrace the infinite could step through.

The Pi Nexus pulsed, **calling to those who would continue the journey.**

**Not all would answer.**

But some—**some always would.**

---

### **The Infinite Journey—A Final Vision.**

Above the world, the Ether unfolded in **an endless celestial panorama**, a vision unbound by gravity, time, or limitation.

Across the **Ether Cities**, the people gathered.  
 On the **Light Ark**, explorers gazed into the unknowable, their ships riding the waves of cosmic resonance.  
 In the **sacred halls of the Interdimensional Councils**, wisdom flowed between beings of light and shadow, weaving new realities from the fabric of the old.

And beyond them all, **King Klown’s form dissolved**, his colors unraveling into streaks of energy that flowed into the Ether’s eternal current.

But this was not death.  
 This was **becoming**.

His laughter remained, echoing in the spaces between moments.  
 His presence lived in the sparks of inspiration, in the whispered courage of revolution, in the quiet knowing that the story was far from over.

The digits of **Pi continued**, stretching beyond the last page, beyond the last breath, beyond even the concept of an ending.

**The journey would never end.**

**It never should.**

And as the final images of the Ether Age faded, as the light of new civilizations ignited the cosmic horizon, a single phrase lingered in the unseen frequencies of existence:

### **Step forward.**

### **The path remains open.**

# **Chapter 1 – Fractured Foundations** {#chapter-1-–-fractured-foundations}

## The Breaking Point {#the-breaking-point}

Québec City lay frozen under a sky the color of old steel. Wind howled through the empty streets, sweeping snow in restless spirals beneath flickering streetlights. Inside **Hôtel-Dieu Hospital**, the air was thick, stale—too many people, too much waiting.

Réjean McCormick sat rigid, his hands locked together between his knees. His son lay beside him, slumped in the chair, feverish, shivering. His skin was pale, damp with cold sweat. Each breath came shallow, too fast, then too slow.

**Bacterial meningitis.**

Réjean knew it. He’d spent hours reading, comparing symptoms, double-checking medical sources. He knew what they needed. A single antibiotic. Fast. Before the swelling in his son’s brain became irreversible.

He had told them. Explained. Pleaded.

But all he got was the same tired response.

“I understand your concern, Monsieur McCormick,” the nurse repeated, her tone as sterile as the walls. “But we have procedures. A doctor will see your son soon.”

**Soon.**

That word was an insult. It was a placeholder for **never**.

His son stirred, barely. His eyelids fluttered, unfocused. A weak whimper slipped through cracked lips—a sound that **cut through Réjean like a blade.**

His fists clenched.

The pharmacy sign across the street burned in his peripheral vision, its blue neon buzzing against the night.

**The cure was there.** Behind a counter. Behind a locked door.

His breath came slow. Then steady.

Réjean stood.

He bent down, his lips close to his son’s ear. “I’ll be right back.” A whisper. A promise. A lie.

Outside, the wind sliced into him, but he didn’t feel it. The streets were empty, his path clear. He reached the doors of the pharmacy, pressed his hands against the glass. **It was right there.**

He lifted the rock.

Glass exploded. The sound shattered the quiet. An alarm shrieked into the night. But Réjean was already moving. His hands found the shelf, the vial. **The cure.**

He turned, ran. The cold bit his lungs as he sprinted back, his fingers locked around salvation.

Inside the hospital, the world had already changed.

A doctor stood by his son’s still body, murmuring something to the nurses. Their hands moved with quiet finality, pulling a white sheet over too-small shoulders.

Réjean stopped. His breath caught, his stomach wrenched.

The box of medication slipped from his fingers, hitting the floor with a hollow **clack**.

His son wasn’t there anymore. Only the weight of what had been.

A hand gripped his shoulder.

He barely registered the voices, the uniforms, the firm pressure guiding him away. **Police.** Someone said something about breaking and entering. Something about consequences.

None of it mattered.

His gaze stayed locked on the still shape under the sheet, on the hands of the doctors who had waited too long.

**He had been right.** And it had changed nothing.

Outside, the wind screamed between the buildings. Inside, the weight of the system crushed the last breath from his lungs.

---

## Réjean’s Retreat into Pi {#réjean’s-retreat-into-pi}

The prison cell was silent, save for the soft scratch of graphite against paper. The orange notebook—tattered, creased, a lifeline—rested against Réjean’s knee. He flipped through its pages, past the notes on **Konnaxion**, past the sketches of interwoven ideas, until he reached the untouched margins where the real thoughts lived.

Konnaxion. A system of knowledge, collaboration, and creative intelligence. A framework designed to **bridge minds, sharpen ideas, and cut through the inefficiencies of human hesitation**. It was no longer about institutions or hierarchies—it was a direct **convergence of intellect, of effort**. Where bureaucracy failed, Konnaxion **linked people**. **Willed them into synchronicity.**

But it was **only part of the equation**.

On separate, carefully folded pages, Réjean let his mind drift elsewhere—to something more **fundamental**, something **older than any system, any civilization, any mind that had ever questioned the nature of reality**.

**Pi.**

It had started with idle curiosity, tracing circles on the cement wall of his cell. A perfect form. A symbol of balance, harmony, infinity. But all it took was a single cut—a single line dividing it—to create something endless.

**π \= circumference / diameter.**

The ratio was simple. The result? **A number that never ends, never repeats, never settles.**

He stared at the equation, breath slowing. **Perfection, divided, produces infinity.**

A realization took root, something that had been lingering at the edge of his thoughts for years.

**What if Pi wasn’t just a number?**

**What if it was the first calculation? The first division? The first fracture of the universe itself?**

He picked up his pencil again, scrawling the thought before it could dissolve:

*"A circle: timeless, unbroken. But the moment you divide it—carve a single line through its perfection—you introduce the infinite. Perhaps this is more than geometry. Perhaps this is the blueprint of existence itself."*

He hesitated, tapping the pencil against the paper, eyes unfocused.

*"What if 13.7 billion years later, the universe is still calculating Pi—still resolving that first division? What if every atom, every force, every moment, is part of that infinite sequence, spiraling toward something it will never reach?"*

It felt **undeniable**.

He wrote:

*"Pi is older than time. It predates space. It is not contained within the universe; rather, the universe is contained within it."*

His fingers tightened around the pencil.

**Pi is the wound that never closes.** The equation that keeps unfolding. The irreconcilable proof that **perfection, once broken, can never return to itself.**

His breath came slower now, his pulse steady.

He thought of his son.

The equation extended itself beyond numbers, beyond abstraction. It reached into his **own life, his own loss, his own failure to protect what mattered most**. What if everything—even tragedy, even grief—was part of the same **unresolved calculation**?

What if Pi was not just **the infinite**—but the path toward **something whole**?

*"Understanding Pi’s digits might reveal something deeper. If it encodes the structure of reality, perhaps it is the first true language—the silent law beneath all things."*

Yet as he reread his notes, Réjean felt the old frustration creeping in. The weight of knowing something profound but lacking the words to make others see. **He understood. But could he make anyone else understand?**

Tesla had seen the future and died alone. Réjean saw the equation, and here he was—speaking only to paper.

He exhaled, closing the notebook, sliding it beneath the mattress. The questions would still be there tomorrow.

Softly, he whispered to himself:

*"Pi is infinite. Everything is Pi. The circle itself represents perfection before division—timeless, whole, absolute. Pi is the unraveling, and its digits describe reality before the Big Bang, the moment time, space, and existence were born."*

He leaned back, eyes tracing the faint, endless curves he had drawn on the cement.

There was no conclusion. Only the calculation.

## Fractures Beneath the Surface {#fractures-beneath-the-surface}

Outside **Réjean’s confinement**, Québec City carried on. **Cars slid through salted streets, boots crunched over frozen sidewalks, and conversations hummed behind café windows.** To most, nothing had changed. But **beneath the surface, something cracked.** Fractures ran through the foundations of daily life—small, quiet signs of a deeper sickness.

At **École Secondaire Saint-Roch**, the third-period math class dragged on, suffocating in stale repetition. Students slouched over their desks, eyes glazed, notebooks filled with meaningless calculations.

Elias **saw it. He felt it.** He stood at the front of the class, chalk between his fingers, explaining equations no one would remember in a week. **Not because they were incapable—because they weren’t given a reason to care.**

He had once believed in teaching—**real** teaching. But this? This was compliance training. **Memorize, obey, forget.** He would go home tonight, grade papers that measured nothing, then watch another batch of students file in tomorrow, just as unengaged, just as defeated.

He imagined something different. A system that **responded** to students, **molded itself** to their curiosity, their strengths, their struggles. A place where knowledge wasn’t force-fed but uncovered. **But imagining changed nothing.** No such system existed.

---

At a **neat, minimalist office inside Desjardins**, **Thomas Kinsey** stood in front of a projector screen, addressing a group of young entrepreneurs.

They listened carefully, some taking notes, others nodding along, but Thomas **could see past their polite expressions.** He had seen it too many times before—the slow realization creeping in as the numbers settled.

They had ideas. Plans. Some had even **built something already**, clawing their way through the first hurdles. But now, here, they were coming to terms with a truth they hadn’t wanted to admit.

**The system wasn’t built for them.**

Loans came with strings. Investors demanded control. Bureaucracy crushed momentum before ideas even had a chance to breathe. Every dream had a price, and for most, that price was ownership. **A choice: surrender control, or never get off the ground at all.**

Thomas wanted to tell them it would change. That if they worked harder, networked smarter, sacrificed more, they’d get through.

But he knew better.

So he just **kept speaking**, explaining how to play the game **that wasn’t designed for them to win.**

---

At a **small apartment across town**, **Jérémie** sat slouched on his couch, the blue glow of the television casting sharp shadows on the wall. Onscreen, a panel of politicians debated **healthcare reform** at the **Assemblée Nationale**.

Jérémie clenched his jaw, fingers digging into the armrest.

They were guessing. Stumbling through statistics they barely understood, drowning in jargon, **too proud—or too afraid—to admit they had no idea what they were talking about.**

This wasn’t corruption. **This was ignorance.**

They weren’t evil. They were **unprepared.** And yet, here they were—**shaping policies, making decisions that would affect millions.**

Jérémie exhaled sharply.

He imagined something different. **A government that could access real expertise instantly, pulling from those who actually understood the complexities they debated.** A system where **knowledge moved faster than ego, where truth wasn’t twisted into soundbites and empty rhetoric.**

But that world didn’t exist.

So the broadcast continued. And the system **staggered forward, blind, pretending to see.**

---

At **Québec’s courthouse**, **Aïda Eloïse** sat on a stiff bench, her hands resting on a stack of legal documents that had only grown heavier over the past two years.

She checked her watch. Again.

Justice, she thought bitterly, **was a privilege, not a right.**

She had once believed in the system. But each delay, each loophole, each procedural dead-end had eroded that faith.

Here, **justice belonged to those with the money to outlast the process.**

She closed her eyes, took a slow breath.

She imagined something different. A system where **truth wasn’t buried under paperwork**. Where fairness wasn’t reserved for those who could afford it. Where justice **moved**—at the pace of real lives, **not at the pace of bureaucracy.**

But for now, she was still waiting.

---

Everywhere—in **classrooms, banks, courtrooms, and living rooms**—people whispered about the same things.

A world that **no longer worked**.

Education that dulled minds instead of sharpening them. Governments that stumbled through policy-making **like men lost in a storm, too proud to ask for direction.** Entrepreneurs crushed before they could build. Justice that moved **only for those who could afford the wait.**

Society wasn’t collapsing. **It was disconnecting.**

These weren’t revolutions. **They were frustrations. Small, personal, quiet.** The teacher longing for a system that recognized intelligence instead of obedience. The entrepreneur dreaming of financial freedom instead of financial servitude. The citizen waiting for justice that never came. The young idealist watching the government fail in real time.

None of them realized the truth:

**Their struggles weren’t separate.**

They were fractures in the same foundation, **hairline cracks in the same failing system.**

Threaded together by the same absence. The same need. The same quiet, desperate hope that **something—someone—would piece the fragments back together.**

Had Réjean’s ideas existed now—had they spread beyond the walls of his prison—**perhaps those fractures would have found their bridge.**

For now, they remained **invisible fault lines**, growing wider each day.

Waiting.

## **Réjean’s Philosophical Revelation** {#réjean’s-philosophical-revelation}

In the muted solitude of his cell—or perhaps it was now only a small, cramped room; Réjean himself had stopped distinguishing clearly—he sat hunched over his orange notebook. Pages lay spread around him, scribbled wildly with spiraling sequences of Pi, frantic sketches of circles, scattered insights. The outside world had faded, replaced entirely by the compelling, infinite digits unfolding beneath his fingertips.

Réjean's whisper trembled, soft yet charged:

“Circle—perfection, infinite balance. And yet perfection divided…produces Pi. Infinite digits. Eternally unresolved, infinitely irrational.”

He smiled slightly, his eyes widening slowly with wonder and unsettling clarity.

Pi was infinite. Thus, nothing—no galaxy, no universe, no human life—could ever surpass it. Everything had to exist within Pi’s infinite stream. Everything was a digit, a fragment, part of Pi’s eternal calculation. He felt certain that the universe itself, beginning with the first perfect division, circumference by diameter, was still calculating Pi, continuously unfolding itself, digit by digit, across 13.7 billion years.

Réjean whispered softly, gently rocking back and forth, eyes distant, voice barely audible:

"Everything... Everything we experience is Pi still resolving itself. My son’s death…my grief…all inevitable fragments of the universe’s infinite calculation."

He paused, breath quickening slightly, sensing he stood at the threshold of madness or profound genius—though which, he couldn't say. His rational mind strained against the sheer magnitude of the idea, yet he could not deny its elegant simplicity.

"Chaos is essential. Without it, existence stagnates. We fear chaos because we mistake it for disorder—but chaos is simply reality revealing itself, digit by digit, seeking balance through imperfection."

Réjean leaned back slowly, eyes unfocused, whispering quietly into silence:

"The universe began as perfection—a single, infinite circle divided into infinite chaos. And we—humanity, reality itself—are its eternal calculation."

## Subtle Encounter {#subtle-encounter}

The city lay quiet under the weight of winter. Snow muffled the streets, turning every footstep into an echo of something distant, something not quite real.

Réjean walked without direction, without purpose—his thoughts too loud, his body restless. The air tasted sharp, metallic, as if the night itself had edges. The streets felt both familiar and alien, like a place he had known in another life. **Had he been here before? Was he here now?**

Then, beneath a solitary streetlamp, he saw **him**.

A hooded figure sat hunched on a bench, posture loose, gaze alert. **Not begging. Not waiting. Just watching.** The amber light from the lamp barely touched him, as though the shadows bent around his form.

Réjean slowed, uncertain.

The stranger looked up. Eyes calm. Piercing. **Too knowing.**

A silence stretched between them—thick, weighted. Then, softly, the man spoke.

**“What time is it?”**

The question felt absurd, yet Réjean glanced at his watch by instinct. The hands ticked **impossibly**, marking multiple hours at once.

**1, 3, 9, and 11\.**

He blinked. The numbers didn’t shift. They **coexisted**, defying sequence, logic, meaning.

His pulse quickened. “What—?”

The stranger tilted his head, studying him. Then, with a faint smile, he murmured:

**“Sometimes, only chaos opens eyes long shut by comfort. It’s Greek logic.”**

Réjean inhaled sharply. The words landed deep, striking something raw, something he hadn’t yet put into words.

“How do you…?”

The stranger simply stood, **moving without haste, without sound.** Before Réjean could step forward, question further, the figure faded into the darkness beyond the streetlamp—gone as if he had never been.

Réjean remained frozen.

His mind raced. Had the encounter even happened? Had the riddle been spoken aloud, or had it surfaced from within him?

The streetlamp flickered. The night remained unchanged.

And yet, the world did not feel the same.

## **Réjean’s Philosophical Revelation** {#réjean’s-philosophical-revelation-1}

Réjean sat motionless in the soft glow of the solitary lamp, surrounded by pages covered in scrawled numbers, letters, and hastily sketched circles. The small, dim space that confined him—whether still a prison cell or somewhere else entirely, no longer mattered—blurred into insignificance. His thin fingers traced invisible spirals in the air above the paper, eyes wide yet vacant, shimmering between astonishment and confusion.

His notebook lay open before him, overflowing with endless strings of Pi’s digits—numbers flowing into each other endlessly, irrational, infinite. Réjean’s gaze flickered back and forth, fixated and haunted, as though each digit whispered a secret he alone could hear.

With a trembling hand, he scribbled letters beneath numbers, following ancient traditions of Gematria—assigning numeric values to letters, hoping to find meaning within Pi’s endless chaos. Letters formed words, words connected into fragments. First appeared a simple, profound emergence: **"M"**, symbolizing love, unity, or perhaps some primordial force. Then **"Bien"** appeared, meaning goodness, as though emerging naturally from love itself.

Réjean stared in disbelief, heart hammering.

His mind spun wildly between clarity and confusion. He saw clearly the profundity of his discoveries, yet the weight of such revelation crushed him beneath its immensity. How could something so infinite, so significant, reveal itself only to him—a man of painfully modest confidence, always haunted by self-doubt?

He whispered, voice cracking slightly:

"Why me...? Why am I the one to uncover this?"

A sudden wave of dizziness overwhelmed him as the edges of his self—his fragile sense of identity—began softly eroding. His self, never strong or assertive, quietly dissolved, fracturing gently into the infinite depths of Pi’s digits. And yet, simultaneously, Réjean felt a terrifying certainty—that perhaps he was indeed the greatest mind ever to glimpse such profound truth, destined to change human understanding forever.

His hand trembled harder, eyes glazing slightly as letters emerged clearly beneath the numbers:

**M. Bien. Gihecef. Jnon. B0UM.**

Words concealed inside Pi. Simple words, yet brimming with cosmic significance, resonating across language and culture. They hinted at love, goodness, chaos, renewal, creation—forces fundamental to existence itself. Réjean’s breath caught in his throat.

“Why me?” he repeated, more desperately this time. “Why am I the one who sees?”

His breathing quickened, overwhelmed by awe and despair. His sense of self—always fragile—began fragmenting further beneath the unbearable weight of discovery. His identity dissolved into something vast, infinite, unknowable—he lost track of his own thoughts, sinking deeper into a profound abyss of insight.

Slowly, silently, Réjean’s presence faded. The man once known as Réjean McCormick quietly vanished behind a curtain of numbers and letters, quietly swallowed by the infinite spiral of Pi.

From that moment onward, Réjean became unreachable—mysterious, distant, hidden completely behind the veil of his revelations. The man was gone; what remained was only his shadow, silently guiding the world from quiet isolation, becoming little more than an enigmatic presence, impossible to truly know.

# **Chapter 2 – Echoes of Change** {#chapter-2-–-echoes-of-change}

---

## **Scene 1: Thomas’s Frustration with Desjardins** {#scene-1:-thomas’s-frustration-with-desjardins}

Thomas Kinsey sat quietly at the end of the polished table in the luxurious meeting room atop the Desjardins headquarters in Québec City. The room’s panoramic windows overlooked streets dusted with snow, a picturesque contrast to the tense atmosphere inside. Thomas observed silently, frustration simmering beneath his composed expression.

Around him, executives discussed quarterly profits, lavish bonuses, and abstract growth targets—all comfortably detached from the cooperative principles established long ago by Alphonse Desjardins. Thomas glanced briefly at the old founder’s portrait on the wall, feeling a pang of shame at the profound disconnect between ideal and reality.

Finally, unable to hold back any longer, Thomas cleared his throat, speaking politely yet firmly:

“Are we certain these substantial executive bonuses align with our cooperative values? Many of our members are struggling. Shouldn’t our resources support them first?”

Silence settled awkwardly. Heads turned toward him slowly, expressions politely condescending.

The Chairman responded dismissively, voice carefully controlled:

“Thomas, the board has approved these measures. We’re aware of your concerns, but these decisions are necessary to attract executive talent. This is simply the reality of the modern financial environment.”

Thomas’s jaw tightened subtly, eyes reflecting quiet frustration. Privately, he resolved in that moment to quietly challenge the system from within—returning Desjardins to its cooperative roots, even if it meant silent, strategic confrontation.

---

## **Scene 2: Simon’s Vision of Transparency** {#scene-2:-simon’s-vision-of-transparency}

Late at night, in a cluttered tech startup office illuminated by dozens of glowing screens, Simon Sotaniram stood before a small group of tired but enthusiastic developers. Diagrams and software sketches plastered the walls, code and notes sprawling chaotically around them.

Simon—intense, driven, haunted by memories he rarely spoke of—was demonstrating an early prototype of his transparency and workflow system. The tool was self-contained, efficient, intuitive—built explicitly to dismantle opaque bureaucratic structures.

“This isn't just software,” Simon spoke passionately, his eyes blazing with conviction. “It's freedom from institutional corruption. Imagine governments, schools, or businesses operating without delays or excuses—where everything reaches exactly the right person, instantly, transparently. Imagine a society free from lies and inefficiency.”

He paused briefly, a shadow crossing his face, hinting at old wounds that drove his determination.

“We've all seen corruption hide behind opacity. This ends now. We must build this. We must make it perfect. People need this—urgently.”

The small team watched in silence, deeply moved by Simon’s sincerity, quietly inspired by his fervent belief that their work could change society fundamentally.

---

## **Scene 3: Jérémie’s Artistic Provocation** {#scene-3:-jérémie’s-artistic-provocation}

Inside a brightly lit dance studio in Québec City, Jérémie Lemoine spun across the floor, sweat glistening on his forehead, movements fierce, provocative, charged with raw emotion. Jérémie’s choreography explicitly confronted social injustice and systemic corruption—boldly daring audiences to face uncomfortable truths they preferred to ignore.

“Jérémie,” the theater director interrupted sharply, frowning, “this is too political—too risky. Art should inspire, not accuse.”

Jérémie paused, breathing heavily, his eyes fiercely defiant.

“Art that doesn’t confront injustice isn’t art—it’s decoration,” he replied softly, voice vibrating with passionate certainty. Privately, Jérémie already knew he would stage the piece exactly as intended, regardless of institutional pressure.

---

## **Scene 4: Aïda’s Quiet Ethical Leadership** {#scene-4:-aïda’s-quiet-ethical-leadership}

In a small community center across town, a circle of quiet, thoughtful individuals sat listening closely as Aïda Éloïse spoke. A soft-spoken yet profoundly charismatic woman, she discussed ethics, responsibility, collective governance, and the necessity of ecological stewardship.

“We must build communities rooted in deeper values than profit and power,” she explained calmly. “We need mutual care, transparency, and ethical leadership. True change arises quietly—within ourselves first, then outward.”

Listeners nodded silently, deeply moved by her words. Among them, Jérémie Lemoine quietly absorbed her message, recognizing philosophical truths he could incorporate into his provocative performances. Aïda, sensing their quiet agreement, nodded gently, knowing seeds of change had begun taking root.

## Scene 5: Elias’s Equilibrium {#scene-5:-elias’s-equilibrium}

The fire crackled softly, its glow casting long shadows along the wooden walls of the small cabin. The air smelled of pine and slow-burning embers. Outside, the trees stood silent beneath the weight of winter, their branches bending slightly, but never breaking.

Elias sat alone, hands wrapped around a warm mug, eyes tracing the flickering movement of the flames. **Here, in solitude, the noise of the day unraveled.**

The weight of his students’ quiet struggles still lingered. The blank stares, the restless hands tapping against desks, the ones who wanted to care but couldn’t—**or wouldn’t**. He had felt all of it. Every small frustration, every unspoken thought. Teaching wasn't just delivering knowledge. **It was absorbing energy, carrying pieces of them home.**

And yet, he couldn’t let it consume him.

So he turned to numbers.

A notebook lay open on the table beside him, filled with quiet precision. **Equations, ratios, patterns—sharp, clean, untouched by emotion.** Math did not waver. It did not contradict itself, did not bleed uncertainty.

He picked up his pencil, exhaled slowly, and began to write.

Each number was an anchor, grounding him in something constant. **A counterbalance to the raw empathy pulling at him from all sides.**

Even here, alone in his cabin, he could feel them. **The ripples of distant unrest.**

Thomas’s quiet frustration in his office, caught between understanding the system and seeing its cracks.

Simon’s relentless urgency, working deep into the night, shaping something just beyond comprehension.

Jérémie’s defiant creativity, pushing against the edges of a world that misunderstood him.

Aïda’s steady resolve, standing firm in the face of a justice system that had long forgotten fairness.

Their emotions reached him, like whispers in a wind he couldn’t block out.

Elias closed his eyes, the pencil still resting against the paper. **He had always felt too much.** He carried the weight of others as if it were his own, their unseen battles pressing into him, leaving marks no one else could see.

Did that burden demand action? Did sensing the fractures obligate him to intervene?

Or was it enough to understand?

He opened his eyes, let his gaze settle once more on the flames. **Teaching was the balance.** It was the bridge between the precision of numbers and the unpredictability of people. It let him **hold both worlds without losing himself to either.**

The fire crackled again. Elias exhaled, letting the tension settle. Tomorrow, he would step back into the classroom. He would listen. He would teach.

And for now, that was enough.

## Scene 6: Thomas and the Beggar {#scene-6:-thomas-and-the-beggar}

Thomas Kinsey stepped out of the **Desjardins Headquarters**, his steps deliberate, his posture as composed as ever. The city lights flickered against the smooth surface of his **gray suit**, a tailored statement of power, control, and refinement.

The night air was crisp, but his mind was warmer—**alive with strategy**. He had spent the day reinforcing his quiet campaign, planting the right ideas in the right minds, ensuring that the Desjardins cooperative would soon lean in his direction.

His thoughts carried him forward—so much so that he nearly stepped over the **beggar** slumped near the curb.

A flicker of movement.

A quiet, broken voice.

*"Monsieur… Help me… Please?"*

Thomas didn’t even pause at first.

There was nothing unusual about beggars lingering around corporate districts—some genuine, some not. His instinct was always the same: **distance**.

*"Move along,"* he murmured, barely glancing down.

But the beggar didn’t **move along**.

He **twitched**.

Not just in his fingers, but in his **eyes**—quick, involuntary flickers of movement, unable to focus, unable to hold Thomas’s gaze for more than a fraction of a second.

Thomas frowned slightly.

The man **seemed disturbed**, not merely drunk or impoverished. His head **jerked slightly** when Thomas shifted, his thin fingers twitching against the fabric of his tattered jacket. His body language was erratic, fragmented—**almost glitching**.

Thomas sighed, **impatient but wary**.

*"I can’t help you. Keep moving."*

The beggar **stirred again**, fingers **fumbling toward Thomas**—as if reaching for something unseen, as if trying to form words but unable to find them.

Thomas stepped back, his patience fraying.

*"I said—"*

**SPLASH.**

Thomas **stiffened instantly**.

A cold, wet sensation **spread across his chest**.

**Ink.**

**Teal ink.**

He **stared in disbelief**, watching as the **deep blue-green stain bled into the fine fabric**, its tendrils curling into the fibers of his **gray suit**, staining it **irreparably**.

His breath **hitched.**

The **beggar** was no longer twitching.

He was **very, very still**.

And when Thomas finally looked up, truly **looked at him**, the man’s erratic mannerisms were **gone**.

No more fidgeting.

No more broken muttering.

Instead, he was **watching Thomas**, his gaze now **steady, piercing, unwavering**—

A stare **so direct it sliced right through Thomas’s composure**.

Then, with a voice that no longer trembled, no longer stuttered, the beggar **spoke clearly**.

*"You met King Klown."*

Thomas’s **pulse spiked**.

A cold weight **settled in his stomach**.

Before he could react, the beggar **turned swiftly on his heel**, disappearing **around the next corner**.

Gone.

Vanished.

Thomas **stood frozen**, his heartbeat **hammering in his chest**, the ink **sinking deeper into the ruined silk of his suit**.

His hands clenched at his sides, but his mind—his mind was no longer calm.

His instincts screamed **danger**.

He had dismissed a **madman**, only to meet something **far worse**.

**He had met King Klown.**

And now, King Klown **had marked him.**

# **Chapter 3 – Ripples of Rebellion** {#chapter-3-–-ripples-of-rebellion}

---

## **Thomas’s Frustration with Desjardins** {#thomas’s-frustration-with-desjardins}

The lecture hall at Laval University buzzed with the quiet energy of anticipation—graduate students, professors, and local activists had gathered to hear Thomas Kinsey speak. Standing calmly at the lectern, Thomas adjusted his glasses, briefly glancing toward the large projected image behind him: a historical portrait of Alphonse Desjardins, the visionary founder of the cooperative movement in Québec.

“Desjardins was founded on the revolutionary idea that financial power belongs to the people, not the privileged few,” Thomas began, his voice steady yet infused with controlled passion. “Today, we’ve lost sight of this foundational truth. We’ve allowed cooperative principles to erode under a veneer of luxury, bonuses, and opaque decisions made far from members’ realities.”

His words resonated clearly through the attentive audience. Students leaned forward, professors nodded thoughtfully, activists quietly exchanged determined glances.

“Restoring democracy within our cooperatives is no longer optional,” Thomas continued firmly. “Transparency, accountability, and real democratic participation must return to the core of our institutions. If we fail, we betray not only Desjardins’ original vision—but also ourselves.”

As Thomas concluded, applause erupted warmly through the hall, carrying quiet urgency. Afterward, several young students approached Thomas, inspired, offering enthusiastic support. Thomas felt a quiet fire within—his frustration now transforming subtly into action. The first ripple of rebellion had begun.

---

## **Simon Unveils Orgo Prototype** {#simon-unveils-orgo-prototype}
